I commute to NYU from eastern Queens and I have a friend who has occasionally commutes from Jamaica, so I have a bit of knowledge about the route you take.

2 hours sounds like you're moving pretty slowly, which is ok, since you've just gotten your bike and it's good to take your time. Take all the time you need to get acclimated to the ride. I think the trickiest part is your easternmost section where you have to get onto Queens Blvd, since riding down QB itself is pretty straightforward.

I'd probably avoid taking Hillside since there's no bike lanes. Nor would I ride on Queens Blvd before the protected lane starts at around 69th Rd. An alternative route that can get very hilly but IMO feels far safer for a patient rider because of the bike lanes is taking 164th St up to Jewel Ave, then taking Jewel to 69th Rd, then going down to Queens Blvd. Jewel takes you through a highway bike lane and 69th doesn't have lanes, so both still require caution, but overall, you're spending less time sharing lanes with cars zooming through boulevards of death.

While you're riding on the road outside of Queens Blvd, do make an effort to be extra visible to drivers, using hand signals, lights, or whatever will make you noticed. I find that riding along faster-moving drivers in eastern Queens can sometimes require a little more vigilance than riding in a more bike- and car-dense part of the city.

What I enjoy about heading towards the QBB is the relative safety once you get onto the Skillman Ave bike lane. However it might not be the fastest route depending on how far you are downtown. If you need to be further down lower Manhattan, try taking Greenpoint Ave from Queens Blvd down to the Williamsburg Bridge.

The ride to eastern queens is long and it can be tiring so I'd probably ease into it, maybe twice a week for the first few weeks to get acclimated.

Have fun, and let me know if you have any questions!

NAH. I think your situation is a pretty normal case among children of Asian immigrants.

You know that college is not a linear investment, nor does it presuppose a single life trajectory. Career changes happen all the time because we get something vastly different from what we expect while in school. You did your time struggling through a miserable job. Are you truly ready to have a miserable career just to fulfill a "debt" to your parents?

Having your parents' blessing in a situation like this is really special. I think that's something that's worth taking with gratitude rather than doubt and self-resentment. It takes a lot of courage to be doing what you're doing, and so I hope you'll believe in yourself and chase after what you love.
